goals: Deepen habitat vocabulary while mixed facts stay sharp.
Build an explorer timeline and keep facts and spelling rolling.
Turn spelling patterns into fluency and hold mixed math.
Re-test the three weak skills and close them for good.

math: mixed x0-x9 multiplication facts and fact families
rounding to the nearest 10 and estimating sums
regrouped addition and the facts you missed
reading: animal coverings: main idea and two details
explorer ships: putting information in order
a favourite passage from weeks 1 to 7
history: the people who built our town
review: helpers, explorers and our state
civics: symbols of our country and what each stands for
ways a kid can help at home, school and in town
who makes a rule and why rules exist
jobs and rules that make a community work
literature: our reader: the main character, the setting and the problem
our reader: explaining the ending in three sentences
our reader: retelling the chapters in order
our reader: drawing one scene with a caption
writing: how one animal covering helps an animal
four sentences using this week's vocabulary
retelling a favourite passage in four sentences
english_grammar: expanding sentences with who, what and where details

coding: a loop that repeats a move four times
a sprite that walks across the screen
a program that makes a choice with a condition
a five-block program built and re-tested

lessons.subject: math
lessons.title: Mixed Facts and Fact Families
lessons.summary: Sort the x0-x9 facts you know from the ones you re-learn, then build two fact families.
lessons.explain: A fact family is three numbers that belong together: 3, 4 and 12 give you 3 x 4 = 12, 4 x 3 = 12 and 12 / 4 = 3. Start by sorting your facts into two piles, know and re-learn. Work the re-learn pile with counters or an array so you can see the groups. Say the fact out loud before you write it, then cover the page and say it again from memory. Speed comes later; the pattern comes first.

examples.q: Build the family for 3, 4 and 12.
steps: Check all three use the same three numbers.

examples.q: 6 x 7 gives 42. What else is true?
steps: Divide the product by one factor.

examples.q: You re-learned 8 x 7. How do you prove it?
examples.a: Draw 8 rows of 7, count the total, then say the family.

practice.question: Which fact family belongs to 5, 6 and 30?
practice.hint: A fact family uses one multiplication, its flip and one division.
practice.praise: Yes! Three numbers, three facts, one family.

practice.question: 9 x 6 = 54. Which division is in the same family?
practice.hint: Divide the product by one factor to get the other.
practice.praise: Yes! 54 shared into 6 groups leaves 9.

practice.question: Which fact should go in the re-learn pile?
options: The one you must count on your fingers
The one you already know cold
The one with the smallest answer
practice.hint: The re-learn pile is for facts that are not automatic yet.
practice.praise: Yes! Re-learn means practise it again.

workbook.prompt: Sort these into know or re-learn: 7 x 8, 2 x 3, 9 x 6, 4 x 5.
workbook.answer: Your own two piles, with a reason beside each fact.

workbook.prompt: Write the full fact family for 4, 7 and 28.
Draw an array that proves 6 x 5 = 30.
workbook.answer: 6 rows of 5 dots, or 5 rows of 6 dots, counted to 30.

workbook.prompt: Name one fact you re-learned today and how you proved it.
workbook.answer: Any fact with the array, counter or family you used to prove it.

lessons.subject: reading
lessons.title: Weekly ELA: Animal Coverings
lessons.summary: Read the nonfiction page on animal coverings, then carry the same text into spelling, grammar and writing.
lessons.explain: Nonfiction writing has a main idea, and the other sentences are details that prove it. Read the page once for fun. Read it again with a pencil and underline the sentence that says what the whole paragraph is about. Then check each other sentence: does it prove that sentence, or does it just sit there? Details that do not attach get cut. The same text runs the whole week: you read it, spell from it, fix sentences from it and finally write from it.

examples.q: Paragraph: A polar bear has hollow hairs that trap warm air. Thick fat underneath keeps the heat in. Both help the bear survive the cold.
examples.a: Main idea: a polar bear has two ways to stay warm.
steps: Find the sentence the others prove.
Check both details attach to it.

examples.q: Detail: The bear looks white. Does it prove the main idea about staying warm?
examples.a: Not on its own, so keep looking for a better detail.
steps: Ask what the main idea claims.
Keep details that prove that claim.

examples.q: New word: camouflage. What do you do first?
examples.a: Read the whole sentence around it; the sentence usually explains it.
steps: Reuse the word in your own sentence.

practice.question: What does a CAPTION tell a reader?
options: What a photo shows and where
practice.hint: A caption is the short line under a photo.
practice.praise: Yes! It names and locates what the photo shows.

practice.question: Where do you look up the meaning of a technical word?
practice.hint: Glossary words are listed in alphabetical order.
practice.praise: Yes! The glossary defines the technical vocabulary.

practice.question: Which sentence is the main idea of a paragraph?
options: The one the other sentences prove
The one with a number in it
practice.hint: Ask what the other sentences are there to support.
practice.praise: Yes! The main idea is the claim the details back up.

workbook.prompt: Underline the main idea sentence in this week's page.
workbook.answer: The sentence the rest of the paragraph proves.

workbook.prompt: Copy two details that prove it.
workbook.answer: Two details that attach directly to that main idea.

workbook.prompt: Write one sentence using this week's word camouflage.
workbook.answer: A full sentence that uses camouflage correctly in meaning.

workbook.prompt: Retell the page in four sentences: first, next, turning point, end.
workbook.answer: Four sentences in the order the page presented them.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.title: Habitats: Camouflage, Hibernation and Migration
lessons.summary: Three ways an animal survives when its habitat changes through the year.
lessons.explain: A habitat has to supply food, water, shelter and space all year, and the year is not the same in every season. Animals answer the hard seasons in three main ways. Camouflage hides an animal from what is looking for it. Hibernation slows an animal right down so it needs almost no food. Migration is a long trip to somewhere warmer and better stocked. None of the three is smarter than the others; each one solves a different problem in a different place.

examples.q: A snowshoe hare turns white in winter. Which survival word is that?
examples.a: Camouflage.
steps: Ask what the change does for the animal.

examples.q: A ground squirrel sleeps through February. Which word?
examples.a: Hibernation.
steps: Notice the food is not there.

examples.q: Geese fly south each autumn. Which word?
examples.a: Migration.

practice.question: Which is camouflage?
options: A moth that looks like tree bark
A bear sleeping in a den
practice.hint: Camouflage is about not being seen.
practice.praise: Yes! Looking like the bark hides the moth.

practice.question: Why does an animal hibernate?
options: To survive a season with almost no food
practice.hint: Think about what winter removes from the habitat.
practice.praise: Yes! Slowing down stretches a thin food supply.

practice.question: Migration is best described as...
options: A long seasonal trip to a better place
practice.hint: Migration involves travel.
practice.praise: Yes! The animal moves instead of waiting.

workbook.prompt: Name the three survival words from today's lesson.
workbook.answer: Camouflage, hibernation and migration.

workbook.prompt: Give one animal example for each word.
workbook.answer: Any valid pair, e.g. hare/camouflage, ground squirrel/hibernation, goose/migration.

workbook.prompt: Label a diagram with where each animal would be in February.
workbook.answer: Hidden in cover, in a den, and in warmer country.

workbook.prompt: Which survival word would help an animal in a hot, dry desert? Why?
workbook.answer: A reasoned choice, e.g. migration away from the dry season.

lessons.subject: history
lessons.title: The People Who Built Our Town
lessons.summary: Put the jobs and events that made a town work into order on a timeline.
lessons.explain: A town does not appear at once; it grows because people take on jobs. Someone surveys the land, someone builds the road, someone runs the store and someone teaches the children. Historians read those jobs the way you read a timeline: in order, and with a reason attached to each step. Ask two questions of every event. What changed because of it, and who benefited? Order first, meaning second. That is how a list of names turns into a story you can defend.

examples.q: A mill is built beside a river in 1840, and a village grows around it. What changed?
examples.a: Jobs and housing arrived, so families settled nearby.

examples.q: Why is the order of a timeline fixed?
examples.a: Nothing can be drawn to the left of something that happened later.

examples.q: Two sources disagree about a date. What do you do?
examples.a: Note both and say which one you trust more, and why.

practice.question: Which comes first on a town timeline?
practice.hint: Timelines run from the past forward.
practice.praise: Yes! Order first, meaning second.

practice.question: Why did early towns grow near rivers?
options: Water, food and a road for trade
practice.hint: Think about what a river gives and what it carries.
practice.praise: Yes! A river is a pantry and a road at once.

practice.question: Who does a historian thank for a fact?
practice.hint: Every historical claim rests on a source.
practice.praise: Yes! Name the source and you can defend the claim.

workbook.prompt: Order four events from this week's lesson on a timeline strip.
workbook.answer: Four events in genuine chronological order, earliest left.

workbook.prompt: Name the job each person did and what it changed.
workbook.answer: A job paired with its consequence, e.g. builder -> road.

workbook.prompt: Add four labels to the town map and read them back.
workbook.answer: Four placed labels read aloud in order.

workbook.prompt: Answer in three sentences: what does our town have that early ones needed?
workbook.answer: Three sentences linking water, food and trade to today.

lessons.subject: math
lessons.title: Four-Digit Addition with Regrouping
lessons.summary: Add four-digit numbers in ones, tens, hundreds and thousands, showing every carry.
lessons.explain: Regrouping is the same trick you learned with two digits, applied four times over. Start at the ones, add, write the digit and carry the ten. Move left to the tens, then the hundreds, then the thousands, and carry each time the column passes ten. Work right to left without skipping, because a carry changes the column on its left. When you finish, estimate first: round both numbers, add the rounded pair, and see whether your answer lands in the right neighbourhood.

examples.q: How do you know the answer is sensible?
examples.a: 400 + 200 is about 600 in hundreds, so about 4,000 overall.
steps: Round each number down and up.

examples.q: You carried into the thousands and got a five-digit answer. When does that happen?
examples.a: When both thousands digits add to ten or more.
steps: If it passes nine, you gain a digit.

practice.hint: Ones 5+9=14 carry 1, tens 7+4+1=12 carry 1.
practice.praise: Yes! Four columns, three carries, one answer.

practice.question: Which step comes first in a four-digit sum?
practice.hint: Always start at the right-hand end.
practice.praise: Yes! Right to left, every time.

practice.hint: Add the thousands digits and keep the three zeros.
practice.praise: Yes! Five thousands and three thousands make eight.

workbook.prompt: Add 4,318 + 2,976 and show every carry.
workbook.answer: 7,294 with carries written above the tens, hundreds and thousands.

workbook.prompt: Estimate each sum before you solve it.
workbook.answer: Rounded pair written first, then the exact answer beside it.

workbook.prompt: Check one sum by subtracting the second number from the total.
workbook.answer: The subtraction returns the first number exactly.

workbook.prompt: Write one word problem that needs a four-digit sum.
workbook.answer: A problem with a real reason to add four-digit amounts.

lessons.subject: reading
lessons.title: Weekly ELA: Ships That Carried Explorers
lessons.summary: Read the ship passage for order and detail, then spell, fix sentences and write from it.
lessons.explain: Informational text often moves in order: what the ship carried, how the crew lived, how they navigated, and why they hugged the coast. Read once for the story. Read again and mark the sequence words, because those words are the skeleton of the piece. Then pull one detail from each part and check it against the text rather than your memory. Finally, use the same passage for spelling and for writing, so one reading carries four subjects instead of four separate trips.

examples.q: Find the sentence that explains why ships stayed near the coast.
examples.a: A coastline is a road that resupplies you.
steps: Read the reason attached to it.

examples.q: What does the word cask mean here?
examples.a: A barrel for holding liquid, read from the words around it.
steps: Read the sentence around the word.
Use the neighbouring words as clues.

examples.q: Order these: striking out, hugging the coast, landfall.
examples.a: Hugging the coast, then striking out, then landfall.

practice.question: Which word best completes: they _____ their position rather than measured it?
practice.hint: Read the contrast: guessing versus measuring.
practice.praise: Yes! The sentence sets guessing against measuring.

practice.question: Sequence words such as first, then and finally help a reader...
practice.hint: Think about what order words do.
practice.praise: Yes! They are the skeleton of informational text.

practice.question: Where do you check a detail you half remember?
practice.hint: The text is the evidence.
practice.praise: Yes! Point to the line that proves it.

workbook.prompt: Underline three sequence words in this week's passage.
workbook.answer: Three words that fix the order of events.

workbook.prompt: Write what the ship carried, in the order the passage gives it.
workbook.answer: The listed items in the original order.

workbook.prompt: Use one word from the passage's pool correctly in a sentence.
workbook.answer: A full sentence using the word with the right meaning.

workbook.prompt: Write four sentences: what the ship carried, how they navigated, why they hugged the coast, and what landfall meant.
workbook.answer: Four sentences covering all four parts of the passage.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.title: Seasons and Weather Patterns
lessons.summary: Why the seasons repeat, and how a weather pattern differs from one day's weather.
lessons.explain: Seasons come from the tilt of the Earth, not from how close the planet is to the Sun. In winter our half of the Earth leans away, so the light arrives at a shallow angle and spreads thin. In summer it leans toward the light and the same energy lands on a smaller patch. Weather is what is happening now; climate is the pattern of weather over years. That is why one cold week does not cancel a season, and why a pattern matters more than a single day.

examples.q: Why is winter colder if the Earth is actually nearer the Sun then?
examples.a: Our hemisphere is tilted away, so the light lands at a shallow angle.

examples.q: Name the four seasons in order.
examples.a: Spring, summer, autumn, winter.
steps: Each season follows the tilt around once.

examples.q: Weather or pattern: it rains most Tuesdays in April.
examples.a: Pattern.
steps: Ask whether it repeats over years.
If yes, it is the pattern.

practice.question: What causes the seasons?
practice.hint: Think about which way the Earth leans.
practice.praise: Yes! The tilt changes the angle of the light.

practice.question: Weather means...
options: what the air is doing today
practice.hint: Weather is short-term.
practice.praise: Yes! Day to day is weather.

practice.question: A pattern is best found by...
options: recording the same measure over many days
practice.hint: Patterns need repeated records.
practice.praise: Yes! Tally it, graph it, then read it.

workbook.prompt: Draw the Earth tilted toward and away from the Sun and label each season.
workbook.answer: Two diagrams with summer on the toward side and winter on the away side.

workbook.prompt: List four weather records worth keeping for two weeks.
workbook.answer: Any four measurable items such as temperature, rainfall, cloud and wind.

workbook.prompt: Sort six statements into weather or pattern.
workbook.answer: Three short-term and three repeating, each with a reason.

workbook.prompt: Explain the seasons to a parent in three sentences without using the word distance.
workbook.answer: Three sentences built on tilt and light angle.

lessons.subject: history
lessons.title: Early Explorers and Their Voyages
lessons.summary: Put the great voyages in order and name what each one changed.
lessons.explain: Explorers sailed for trade routes, not for the sake of a new place. Columbus wanted a westward path to Asia and met two continents instead. Vasco da Gama went around Africa and reached India by sea. Magellan's crew completed the first circumnavigation, though Magellan himself did not. Read each voyage as a claim: who funded it, what they expected, and what actually happened. When the expectation and the outcome differ, that gap is where the history gets interesting.

examples.q: 1492: Columbus sails west. What did he expect?
examples.a: A sea route to Asia.

examples.q: Who reached India by sea first?
examples.a: Vasco da Gama, in 1498, around Africa.

examples.q: Why order the voyages before discussing them?
examples.a: Later voyages learned from earlier failures.

practice.question: Explorers first crossed the Atlantic because they wanted...
practice.hint: Trade drove the voyages.
practice.praise: Yes! The new land was a means, not the plan.

practice.question: Which explorer's crew completed the first trip around the world?
practice.hint: Magellan died on the way; his crew finished.
practice.praise: Yes! The crew completed what the captain began.

practice.question: A dated voyage line on a map tells a historian...
options: when a place became known to that country
practice.hint: Dates are the point of the line.
practice.praise: Yes! Date plus route is a checkable claim.

workbook.prompt: Order four voyages from this week's lesson on a timeline.
workbook.answer: Four voyages in genuine chronological order, earliest left.

workbook.prompt: For one explorer, write: sponsor, expectation, outcome.
workbook.answer: Three labelled lines that do not contradict the lesson.

workbook.prompt: Label the route on a blank map and read the labels back.
workbook.answer: A route line with a date at each end.

workbook.prompt: Answer in three sentences: what did explorers change for people at home?
workbook.answer: Three sentences on trade, knowledge or goods.

lessons.subject: math
lessons.title: Rounding to the Nearest 10
lessons.summary: Round two-digit numbers to the nearest ten, then use the rounded pair to estimate a sum.
lessons.explain: Rounding asks which ten a number lives closer to. Look at the ones digit. Five or more rounds the tens digit up; four or less leaves it alone. A number line makes this visible: 47 sits between 40 and 50, closer to 50, so it rounds up. Estimating before you compute gives you a sanity check. If your exact answer and your estimate disagree wildly, one of them is wrong, and it is usually quicker to find out which by re-estimating than by re-adding.

examples.q: Round 47 to the nearest ten.
steps: 7 is five or more, so round up.

examples.q: Round 82 to the nearest ten.
steps: 2 is less than five, so stay.

examples.q: Estimate 53 + 36.
examples.a: About 90.

practice.question: Round 65 to the nearest 10.
practice.hint: Five or more rounds up.
practice.praise: Yes! The ones digit is 5, so round up.

practice.question: Round 34 to the nearest 10.
practice.hint: Four or less stays.
practice.praise: Yes! 34 sits closer to 30.

practice.question: Which estimate is closest to 71 + 18?
practice.hint: Round each number first.

workbook.prompt: Round ten two-digit numbers to the nearest ten.
workbook.answer: Ten correct roundings, each with the ones digit circled.

workbook.prompt: Plot 47 on a number line between 40 and 50.
workbook.answer: A mark closer to 50, labelled 47.

workbook.prompt: Estimate three sums, then compute them exactly.
workbook.answer: An estimate and an exact answer for each, and a note on how close they are.

workbook.prompt: Explain the rounding rule in your own words.
workbook.answer: Five or more rounds up; four or less stays, with a reason.

lessons.subject: reading
lessons.title: Weekly ELA: Reading a Weather Map
lessons.summary: Decode a diagram-heavy nonfiction page, then carry its vocabulary into spelling and writing.
lessons.explain: A weather map is a diagram, and diagrams carry more information than the paragraph beside them. Learn the code first: lines with triangles are cold fronts, lines with semicircles are warm fronts, and crowded loops mean brisk wind. Words like isobar and front are technical, so read the sentence around them before you reach for a glossary. Once the code is decoded, the map stops being a doodle and becomes an argument between air masses that you can follow.

examples.q: A blue line with triangles on a weather map is...
examples.a: A cold front, with triangles pointing the way it moves.

examples.q: Crowded isobars mean...
examples.a: Brisk wind.
steps: Closer together means a steeper pressure difference.

examples.q: What does front mean here, given the sentence about air masses?
examples.a: The boundary where two air masses meet.
steps: Take the meaning the sentence supports.

practice.question: In this passage, a front is...
options: the boundary between two air masses
practice.hint: The sentence about arguing air masses gives it away.
practice.praise: Yes! Context picks the meaning.

practice.question: Crowded isobars tell you the wind is...
practice.hint: Spacing on the map carries meaning.
practice.praise: Yes! Close loops mean a strong difference.

practice.question: A diagram is...
options: a labelled picture that carries real information
practice.hint: Read the labels and leader lines.
practice.praise: Yes! Never decoration, always a shortcut.

workbook.prompt: Name the four symbols on this week's map and what each means.
workbook.answer: Cold front, warm front, isobar and temperature number, each with its meaning.

workbook.prompt: Write the definition of isobar in your own words.
workbook.answer: A loop of equal pressure, with spacing showing wind strength.

workbook.prompt: Caption the diagram in one sentence.
workbook.answer: One sentence naming what the diagram shows.

workbook.prompt: Write four sentences explaining how to read the map to a new student.
workbook.answer: Four ordered sentences a new reader could follow.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.title: Weather Tools and Forecasts
lessons.summary: Match each tool to the measure it makes, and read a forecast as a prediction with odds.
lessons.explain: Weather is measurement before it is prediction. A thermometer reads temperature, a rain gauge reads rainfall, a wind vane shows direction and an anemometer reads speed. A barometer reads pressure, and falling pressure is the classic hint that weather is about to turn. A forecast chains those measures into a claim about tomorrow, and a forecast is always a probability, never a promise. Read one with a question in mind: which measure supports it, and how confident is the wording?

examples.q: Which tool tells you wind direction?
examples.a: A wind vane.
steps: Name the tool that reads it.

examples.q: Pressure is falling and the sky is greying. What do you predict?
examples.a: Rain is likely, because falling pressure accompanies incoming weather.
steps: State the odds, not a certainty.

examples.q: Why is a forecast a probability?
examples.a: It is built from measures that can shift between now and then.

practice.question: A rain gauge measures...
practice.hint: Think of what collects in it.
practice.praise: Yes! It collects and measures rainfall.

practice.question: A wind vane shows...
practice.hint: It points into the wind.
practice.praise: Yes! Direction, not speed.

practice.question: A barometer reads...
practice.hint: Falling pressure hints at a change.
practice.praise: Yes! Pressure is the forecasting workhorse.

workbook.prompt: Match five tools to the measure each one makes.
workbook.answer: Five correct tool-to-measure pairs.

workbook.prompt: Record temperature and rainfall for four days in a table.
workbook.answer: A four-row table with two columns of readings.

workbook.prompt: Write a one-sentence forecast and name the measure behind it.
workbook.answer: A forecast sentence plus the reading that supports it.

workbook.prompt: Graph the four days of rainfall as a bar graph.
workbook.answer: Four bars with a labelled axis.

lessons.subject: history
lessons.title: Explorers and Their Routes
lessons.summary: Trace each route on a map, date it, and say what the route made possible.
lessons.explain: A route is a decision, and every decision has a reason. Sailing around Africa avoided overland taxes; sailing west risked an ocean nobody could cross with confidence. Trace each route with a finger, add a date at each end, and then ask what the route changed for people at home. Goods got cheaper, maps got corrected, and some places were named by people who had names already. Good history notes both: what the route opened, and what it cost.

examples.q: Why sail around Africa rather than march overland?
examples.a: Sea freight avoided taxes and delays on land.

examples.q: What belongs at each end of a route line?
examples.a: A place name and a date.

examples.q: What did early maps get wrong?
examples.a: Coastlines, distances and names, corrected by later voyages.

practice.question: A route line on a map is most useful when it carries...
practice.hint: Without dates a route proves nothing.
practice.praise: Yes! Date plus place is the evidence.

practice.question: Why did sailing around Africa matter?
options: It opened a sea route to India's trade
practice.hint: Think about what the route reached.
practice.praise: Yes! It connected Europe to Indian Ocean trade.

practice.question: What is a historian's first step with a route?
options: Put it in order with the others
practice.hint: Order first, meaning second.
practice.praise: Yes! Sequence comes before explanation.

workbook.prompt: Trace this week's route on a blank map and date both ends.
workbook.answer: A traced line with a place and a year at each end.

workbook.prompt: Name one thing the route opened and one thing it cost.
workbook.answer: One gain and one cost, both stated plainly.

workbook.prompt: Add four labels to the timeline and read them back.
workbook.answer: Four dated labels read aloud in order.

workbook.prompt: Answer in three sentences: why do routes matter to historians?
workbook.answer: Three sentences about evidence, dates and consequences.

lessons.subject: math
lessons.title: Regrouped Addition and Missed Facts
lessons.summary: Re-teach the two weakest categories, then re-test cold with no practice first.
lessons.explain: A checkpoint is not a punishment; it is a way of finding the exact hole so you can close it. Start by sorting your work from weeks one to seven into categories: facts, regrouped addition, word problems. Count the misses in each. Take the two worst categories and work four items each with a model beside you. Then stop practising and take ten cold items, because the only honest measure of a skill is what you can do before you warm up.

examples.q: You missed four facts and six regrouped sums. Where do you start?
examples.a: Regrouped sums, because that is the larger hole.

examples.q: Why test cold?
examples.a: Warming up hides which skills are actually secure.

examples.q: What counts as fixed?
examples.a: The same skill right twice, a day apart.

practice.question: Which is the fairest check of a skill?
options: Ten items with no practice first
Ten items after an hour of drilling
practice.hint: Cold testing hides nothing.
practice.praise: Yes! Cold items measure what is secure.

practice.hint: Ones 6+7=13 carry 1, tens 5+6+1=12 carry 1.
practice.praise: Yes! Two carries, one answer.

practice.question: A skill counts as fixed when...
options: you get it right twice a day apart
practice.hint: One success can be luck.
practice.praise: Yes! Spaced success is the honest bar.

workbook.prompt: Sort this week's misses into three categories and count them.
workbook.answer: Three labelled piles with a count in each.

workbook.prompt: Work four modelled items in your weakest category.
workbook.answer: Four items with the model shown beside each.

workbook.prompt: Take ten cold items and record the score.
workbook.answer: Ten items attempted without practice first, score recorded.

workbook.prompt: Name the one skill you will re-test tomorrow.
workbook.answer: One specific skill, not a subject name.

lessons.subject: reading
lessons.title: Weekly ELA: The Week the Reading Log Changed
lessons.summary: Read a narrative about a rule changing, then carry its vocabulary into spelling and writing.
lessons.explain: This passage reads like a story but argues like an essay, which is what a personal narrative does when it earns its point. Read it once for what happened. Read again and mark the moment the rule changed, then find the sentence that says why it mattered. Ask what the change cost, since every change costs something, and what it produced. Finally, use its words for spelling and write four sentences of your own about a rule you would change, with your reason attached.

examples.q: What was the old rule, and what replaced it?
examples.a: Title and page became one thing that happened.

examples.q: Why did the fake log become true?
examples.a: The new column asked for something the book had to supply.

examples.q: What is the last sentence doing?
examples.a: Generalising the small change into a claim about improvements.
steps: Read the claim built on it.

practice.question: The reading log improved because...
options: a student named the missing piece
practice.hint: Find who spoke up.
practice.praise: Yes! Ari named what the log never asked for.

practice.question: A personal narrative can also...
practice.hint: This piece tells a story to prove something.
practice.praise: Yes! Story in service of a claim.

practice.question: The phrase a margin means the change was...
options: small enough to fit beside the text

lessons.subject: science
lessons.title: Animal Groups Review
lessons.summary: Sort animals into groups by how they are born and what covers their bodies.
lessons.explain: Scientists group animals by shared traits, and the two traits that do the most work are how young are born and what covers the body. Mammals have hair and feed milk. Birds have feathers and lay hard-shelled eggs. Reptiles have scales and mostly lay eggs on land. Fish have scales and gills and stay in water. Amphibians start in water with gills and later breathe air. A group is a hypothesis: if you find an animal that fits none of the five, the group list needs revisiting.

examples.q: A bat feeds milk and has hair. Which group?
examples.a: Mammal, even though it flies.

examples.q: A frog starts with gills and later breathes air.
examples.a: Amphibian.

examples.q: Why group at all?
examples.a: So a new animal's traits can be predicted from its group.

practice.question: Which animal is a mammal?
practice.hint: Hair and milk are the deciding traits.
practice.praise: Yes! Dolphins breathe air, have hair and feed milk.

practice.question: Feathers belong to which group?
practice.hint: Only one group has them.
practice.praise: Yes! Feathers are unique to birds.

practice.question: An amphibian typically...
options: starts in water with gills and later breathes air
practice.hint: Look for the change of breathing.
practice.praise: Yes! The switch from gills to lungs is the marker.

workbook.prompt: Sort eight animals into the five groups.
workbook.answer: Eight animals each placed in a defensible group.

workbook.prompt: Write the two deciding traits for each group.
workbook.answer: Body covering and how the young are born, for each group.

workbook.prompt: Draw one animal from each of three groups and label the trait.
workbook.answer: Three drawings with the matching trait labelled.

workbook.prompt: Explain to a parent why a bat is not a bird.
workbook.answer: Three sentences built on hair and milk rather than feathers.

lessons.subject: history
lessons.title: Review: Helpers, Explorers and Our State
lessons.summary: Rebuild the quarter's timeline, name the sources, and fix anything that no longer holds.
lessons.explain: A review is a reconstruction, not a re-read. Take a blank timeline and put the quarter's events on it from memory. Then open the lessons and check each placement. Anything you got wrong is the useful part of the exercise, because a corrected error sticks better than a rehearsed one. Finish by naming the source for three of the events. Facts you can source are facts you can defend; facts you only recall are facts you are renting.

examples.q: You place a voyage in the wrong decade. What now?
examples.a: Note the correction and why the mistake happened.

examples.q: What makes a source better?
examples.a: Closer to the event, dated, and checkable against another source.

examples.q: Name the three strands this quarter covered.
examples.a: Community helpers, explorers, and our state.

practice.question: The best first step in a review is...
options: rebuild it from memory, then check
practice.hint: Retrieval shows you the holes.
practice.praise: Yes! Memory first, notes second.

practice.question: Which source is strongest for a town's founding?
options: A dated council record from that year
practice.hint: Dated and close to the event wins.
practice.praise: Yes! Contemporaneous and checkable.

practice.question: Records of the past are kept so that...
options: we can trace how the town changed
practice.hint: Records are evidence of change.
practice.praise: Yes! That is history at town level.

workbook.prompt: Rebuild the quarter's timeline from memory, then correct it.
workbook.answer: A first pass, a checked pass, and the corrections marked.

workbook.prompt: Name a source for three events and say why you trust each.
workbook.answer: Three sources with a stated reason for each.

workbook.prompt: Write one sentence for each of the three strands.
workbook.answer: Three sentences, one per strand, each accurate.

workbook.prompt: Name the skill you most need to re-test and why.
workbook.answer: One specific skill with a reason drawn from your own work.

passages.title: Animal Coverings
passages.text: Every animal is dressed for its own weather. A polar bear has hollow hairs that trap warm air against its skin, and a layer of fat underneath holds the heat in. A desert beetle carries a bumpy shell that collects fog, so the water beads up and rolls straight to its mouth. A chameleon does not change colour to match the wall; it changes colour to show how it feels and how warm it is. A fish is covered in overlapping scales that lie flat and let it slip through the water. Coverings are not decoration. Feathers, fur, scales and shells each solve one problem: stay the right temperature, stay hidden, or stay moving.

passages.title: Ships That Carried Explorers
passages.text: Five hundred years ago a ship going west was a floating town. It carried barrels of water, salted meat, hard biscuit, rope, spare sailcloth and a cask of wine. Sailors slept on deck in foul weather and below deck in calm, in a space barely longer than a classroom. They navigated by the sun at noon and by the North Star at night, guessing their position rather than measuring it. Most voyages hugged the coast for weeks before striking out, because a coastline is a road that resupplies you. The ships were small, the oceans were not, and every landfall was a rumour until it was not.

passages.title: Reading a Weather Map
passages.text: A weather map looks like a doodle until you learn the code. A blue line with triangles is a cold front, and the triangles point the way it is moving. A red line with semicircles is a warm front. Where the two meet, air masses argue, and the argument is what we call weather. Numbers on the map are temperatures in the same units everywhere, so a cold 4 in the north and a mild 14 in the south tell one story. Isobars are the squiggly loops: when they crowd together the wind is brisk, and when they spread out the day is still. The map is a snapshot taken at one hour, so tomorrow it will have moved on.

passages.title: The Week the Reading Log Changed
passages.text: For six weeks our reading log had one rule: write the title and the page. Then Ari pointed out that the log never asked what the book was about, so half the class copied the title off the cover and guessed the rest. We added a single column called one thing that happened. The next week the log filled up with real sentences, and two people asked for books nobody had recommended. The change was small enough to fit in a margin. That is usually how improvements work: someone names the missing piece, the group writes it down, and the thing that was fake becomes true.
